arXiv:2602.07120v1 [cs.CL] 06 Feb 2026

Anchored Decoding:
Provably Reducing Copyright Risk for Any Language Model

Jacqueline He Affiliation: University of Washington Correspondence to: jyyh@cs.washington.edu    Jonathan Hayase Affiliation: University of Washington    Wen-tau Yih Affiliation: University of Washington    Sewoong Oh Affiliation: University of Washington    Luke Zettlemoyer Affiliation: University of Washington    Pang Wei Koh Affiliation: University of Washington Affiliation: Allen Institute for Artificial Intelligence
Abstract

Modern language models (LMs) tend to memorize portions of their training data and emit verbatim spans. When the underlying sources are sensitive or copyright-protected, such reproduction raises issues of consent and compensation for creators and compliance risks for developers. We propose Anchored Decoding, a plug-and-play inference-time method for suppressing verbatim copying: it enables decoding from any risky LM trained on mixed-license data by keeping generation in bounded proximity to a permissively trained safe LM. Anchored Decoding adaptively allocates a user-chosen information budget over the generation trajectory and enforces per-step constraints that yield a sequence-level guarantee, enabling a tunable risk–utility trade-off. To make Anchored Decoding practically useful, we introduce a new permissively trained safe model (TinyComma 1.8B), as well as AnchoredByte Decoding, a byte-level variant of our method that enables cross-vocabulary fusion via the ByteSampler framework (Hayase et al., 2025). We evaluate our methods across six model pairs on long-form evaluations of copyright risk and utility. Anchored and AnchoredByte Decoding define a new Pareto frontier, preserving near-original fluency and factuality while eliminating up to 75% of the measurable copying gap (averaged over six copying metrics) between the risky baseline and a safe reference, at a modest inference overhead.

Keywords: 
copyright, LLMs, decoding

1 Introduction

The remarkable capabilities of modern language models (LMs) are fundamentally tied to the scale and diversity of their pre-training data. These corpora are often harvested from the open web with minimal filtering, and may contain sensitive or copyright-protected documents (Kandpal et al., 2025). LMs are able to memorize spans seen during pre-training and later emit them at inference time (Carlini et al., 2021; Carlini et al., 2023; Karamolegkou et al., 2023). Such reproduction is often unauthorized and uncompensated with respect to the original creators (Kandpal & Raffel, 2025), and may expose developers to legal and privacy liabilities (Henderson et al., 2023). Remediation is difficult, as filtering data for sensitive documents and re-training frontier models is prohibitively expensive. Further, as copyrighted material is usually higher quality, its wholesale exclusion can significantly compromise end performance (Meeus et al., 2024).

We address this problem with Anchored Decoding, a practical inference-time method that interpolates between the next-token distributions of a safe model and a higher-utility risky model. Formally, a safe model is trained exclusively on public domain and openly licensed text (Open Knowledge Foundation, 2015). While this ecosystem is still nascent, it is expanding with the recent release of permissively licensed pre-training corpora (Min et al., 2024; Bommarito II et al., 2025; Kandpal et al., 2025; Langlais et al., 2025). Conversely, a risky language model is trained on mixed-license sources that may include copyrighted or otherwise sensitive documents; almost all open-weight (Grattafiori et al., 2024; Qwen Team, 2024; Gemma Team et al., 2025; Meta AI, 2025) and closed-weight (Anthropic, 2024; OpenAI et al., 2024; Gemini Team et al., 2025) LMs belong in this category. Safe LMs offer stronger compliance at the cost of performance (Kandpal et al., 2025), whereas risky LMs offer greater utility but a higher risk of regurgitation. Fig. 1(a) illustrates this trade-off: given the start of a popular novel, the risky LM generates its verbatim continuation, while the safe LM avoids reproduction but yields a qualitatively less fluent output.

At each decoding step, Anchored Decoding computes a closed-form fusion of the risky and safe next-token distributions by choosing interpolation weights that satisfy a local divergence budget relative to the safe model. We show these local constraints compose into a sequence-level guarantee that provably satisfies the KK-NAF criterion (Vyas et al., 2023), a mathematical measure that enforces a user-chosen budget KK on divergence from the generated distribution to the safe model, thereby providing a principled control on copyright leakage risk. We further introduce two empirically effective adjustments that account for the non-uniform nature of distributional risk across generation: first, a one-time, prompt-dependent prefix debt that reduces the initial budget based on how strongly the input prompt appears to have already been memorized by the risky LM, and second, an adaptive banking rule that saves unspent budget from low-risk steps for occasional high-risk spikes later in generation.

Returning to Fig. 1(a), Anchored Decoding produces a continuation that avoids reproduction while remaining fluent and plausible. Our decoding strategy is training-free, provides a user-controllable tradeoff knob with a formal bound, and retrofits to any off-the-shelf LM with exposed logits. Anchored Decoding holds less restrictive assumptions compared to prior two-model copyright mitigation approaches: it does not require a hand-curated list of seed words (TokenSwap (Prashant et al., 2025)), nor does it require the stringent model-pair construction assumed by CP-Fuse (e.g., disjoint training shards), beyond access to a permissively trained safe anchor  (Abad et al., 2025).

We next turn from method-level assumptions to a more fundamental constraint. Many two-model fusion methods, including Anchored Decoding, assume a shared vocabulary. This requirement is quite restrictive for copyright mitigation, as state-of-the-art safe models (e.g., Comma 7B (Kandpal et al., 2025)) employ bespoke tokenization schemes that render direct token-level fusion infeasible. We address this bottleneck via two contributions: first, to enable token-level vocabulary alignment, we release TinyComma 1.8B, a compact variant of the Comma architecture, that is pre-trained exclusively on 169.5B tokens of openly licensed data from the Common Pile (Kandpal et al., 2025). By design, TinyComma 1.8B adopts the Llama 3.1 tokenizer (Grattafiori et al., 2024), facilitating direct compatibility with the Llama 3.1 family. Second, we introduce AnchoredByte Decoding, a byte-level, KK-NAF compliant analogue of Anchored Decoding. AnchoredByte Decoding builds upon the ByteSampler framework (Hayase et al., 2025) and bypasses tokenizer mismatch by operating on the next-byte distribution. Together, these advances support a significantly broader range of model pairs than previously possible.

When evaluated in realistic long-form settings, Anchored and AnchoredByte Decoding consistently achieve Pareto-optimality against strong mitigation baselines across six model pairs. They attain near-original fluency and factuality while closing up to 75% of the reduction between the risky baseline and safe reference. For example, we show risk-utility tradeoff plots in Fig. 1(b) for the model pair {TinyComma 1.8B, Llama 3.1 70B} (decoding at the token level). Anchored Decoding adds modest inference overhead (e.g., only 1.1x in this case) by pairing risky LMs with a much smaller safe LM, making the second forward pass relatively cheap without sacrificing effectiveness. We further analyze why Anchored Decoding works: our key intuition is that the per-step KL divergence between the risky and safe models is a useful signal for identifying when generation has entered a copyright-sensitive regime. Beyond copyright mitigation in LMs, Anchored Decoding is agnostic to tokenizer, modality, and domain. Our framework serves as a general-purpose tool that is applicable wherever a high-capability generative process must be rigorously bounded by a trusted reference distribution.

2 Preliminaries

We consider token-level autoregressive language models pp that operate over a fixed vocabulary 𝒱\mathcal{V}. Given a prompt sequence xx, define a probability distribution over variable-length token sequences y0:T−1y_{0:T-1} with yt∈𝒱y_{t}\in\mathcal{V} as

p(y0:T−1∣x)=∏t=0T−1p(yt∣y<t,x)for T≤Tmax,\displaystyle p(y_{0:T-1}\mid x)=\prod_{t=0}^{T-1}p(y_{t}\mid y_{<t},x)\quad\text{for }T\leq T_{\max}, (1)

where yT−1=EOSy_{T-1}=\textrm{EOS} denotes termination. We assume access to a safe model psp_{s} trained only on permissively licensed text, and a more performant risky model prp_{r} that may reproduce copyrighted data due to its broader, unchecked training set. prp_{r} and psp_{s} are assumed to induce the same support over 𝒱\mathcal{V}, which are typically satisfied by standard softmax parameterizations. Our goal is to find some target distribution that balances the competing objectives of copyright safety (from psp_{s}) and utility (from prp_{r}).

KK-Near Access-Freeness (KK-NAF).

First, we formally define our desired copyright safety condition. We adopt the KK-NAF framework introduced by Vyas et al. (2023), which bounds the total divergence over the entire distribution of sequences generated by a model pp relative to a safe model psp_{s}:

Definition 2.1.

[Global KK-NAF] Let K≥0K\geq 0 be a global information budget. Formally, a model pp satisfies the global KK-NAF guarantee (relative to psp_{s}) if, for every input sequence xx and every T≤TmaxT\leq T_{\max},

𝒟(p(y<T∣x)∥ps(y<T∣x))≤K,\displaystyle\mathcal{D}\!\left(p(y_{<T}\mid x)\,\big\|\,p_{s}(y_{<T}\mid x)\right)\leq K, (2)

where y<T=(y0,…,yT−1)y_{<T}=(y_{0},\dots,y_{T-1}), and 𝒟\mathcal{D} is some arbitrary divergence function. We primarily consider 𝒟=DK​L\mathcal{D}=D_{KL}, the Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence (Kullback & Leibler, 1951).11 1 For generality, we show that the guarantees to our method also hold when setting 𝒟\mathcal{D} as the ∞\infty-Rényi divergence in Sec. B.3, and show experimental ablations in Sec. 5.2. Throughout, we write p(⋅∣x)p(\cdot\mid x) as shorthand for the autoregressive model pp and its induced finite-horizon prefix distributions {p⁡(y<T∣x)}T≤Tmax\{p(y_{<T}\mid x)\}_{T\leq T_{\max}}.

3 Anchored Decoding

3.1 A Tractable Token-Level Approximation

Our goal is to construct a new distribution p∗p^{*} that approximates prp_{r} to maximize utility, while remaining strictly subject to the safety constraint relative to psp_{s} (Definition 2.1). This yields the constrained sequence-level optimization:

p∗=arg​minp\displaystyle p^{*}=\argmin_{p}\quad DK​L(p(⋅∣x)∥pr(⋅∣x))\displaystyle D_{KL}\big(p(\cdot\mid x)\,\|\,p_{r}(\cdot\mid x)\big) (3)
s.t. DK​L(p(⋅∣x)∥ps(⋅∣x))≤K.\displaystyle D_{KL}\big(p(\cdot\mid x)\,\|\,p_{s}(\cdot\mid x)\big)\leq K.

As Eq. 3 is defined at the sequence level, solving this directly is computationally intractable, as it becomes a search problem over the exponentially large 𝒱Tmax\mathcal{V}^{T_{\max}}.

Therefore, similar to Abad et al. (2025), we approximate the global objective by decomposing the problem into a series of local (per-token) objectives. Concretely, rather than solving for an optimal sequence-level spending schedule subject to a global budget KK, we impose a per-step budget ktk_{t} at each timestep tt. The sequence-level constraint in Eq. 3 can be decomposed via the chain rule of KL divergence into a sum of per-step conditional divergences. Accordingly, at each tt and for any prefix y<t∼p∗(⋅|x)y_{<t}\sim p^{*}(\cdot|x) generated thus far, we solve a local constrained problem to obtain an optimal next-token distribution, pt∗(⋅∣y<t,x)p_{t}^{*}(\cdot\mid y_{<t},x), that stays within the per-step budget ktk_{t} relative to psp_{s}, while drawing close to prp_{r}:

pt∗(⋅∣y<t,x)=\displaystyle p_{t}^{*}(\cdot\mid y_{<t},x)= argminp∈Δ⁡(𝒱)DK​L(p∥pr(⋅∣y<t,x))\displaystyle\arg\min_{p\in\Delta(\mathcal{V})}\;D_{KL}\!\big(p\,\|\,p_{r}(\cdot\mid y_{<t},x)\big) (4)
s.t.DK​L(p∥ps(⋅∣y<t,x))≤kt,\displaystyle\text{s.t.}\quad D_{KL}\!\big(p\,\|\,p_{s}(\cdot\mid y_{<t},x)\big)\leq k_{t},
∑y∈𝒱p⁡(y)=1,p⁡(y)>0∀y∈𝒱.\displaystyle\sum_{y\in\mathcal{V}}p(y)=1,\quad p(y)>0\ \ \forall y\in\mathcal{V}.

By the chain rule for KL, any continuation generated autoregressively by {pt∗(⋅|y<t,x)}t<Tmax\{p_{t}^{*}(\cdot|y_{<t},x)\}_{t<T_{\max}} of length T≤TmaxT\leq T_{\max} satisfies Definition 2.1, as the following theorem shows:

Theorem 3.1 (Safety of local approximation).

Let p∗p^{*} be a sequence-level distribution defined autoregressively by p∗​(y<T|x)=∏t=0T−1pt∗​(yt|y<t,x)p^{*}(y_{<T}|x)=\prod_{t=0}^{T-1}p_{t}^{*}(y_{t}|y_{<t},x). If, for all decoding steps t<Tmaxt<T_{\max}, the conditional distribution pt∗p_{t}^{*} solves Eq. 4 with a per-step budget ktk_{t} such that ∑t=0Tmax−1kt≤K\sum_{t=0}^{T_{\max}-1}k_{t}\leq K, then p∗p^{*} satisfies the global KK-NAF guarantee in Eq. 3 for all T≤TmaxT\leq T_{\max}.

In effect, our approximation yields a valid solution to the original optimization. We further note a simple corollary:

Corollary 3.2 (Constant per-step cap).

Setting kt≡kk_{t}\equiv k for all t<Tmaxt<T_{\max} satisfies the condition of Theorem 3.1 whenever k​Tmax≤Kk\,T_{\max}\leq K.

3.2 Solving for a fused distribution pt∗p^{*}_{t}

Eq. 4 admits a closed-form solution that can be efficiently computed at each decoding step:

Proposition 3.3 (Solving for pt∗p_{t}^{*}).

For a given local budget ktk_{t} at decoding step tt, the optimal distribution pt∗p_{t}^{*} that solves Eq. 4 is a weighted geometric mean:

pt∗=1Zps(⋅∣y<t,x)λ1+λpr(⋅∣y<t,x)11+λ,\displaystyle p_{t}^{*}=\frac{1}{Z}p_{s}(\cdot\mid y_{<t},x)^{\frac{\lambda}{1+\lambda}}p_{r}(\cdot\mid y_{<t},x)^{\frac{1}{1+\lambda}}, (5)

where ZZ is a normalization constant and λ≥0\lambda\geq 0 is the dual variable (Lagrange multiplier) associated with the KL constraint.

In practice, determining the optimal λ\lambda (equivalently, the mixing weight λ1+λ\frac{\lambda}{1+\lambda}) reduces to a 1D root-finding problem. When the constraint is active, we solve for λ≥0\lambda\geq 0 such that f(λ):=DK​L(pt∗(λ)∥ps,t)−kt=0f(\lambda):=D_{KL}\bigl(p_{t}^{*}(\lambda)\,\|\,p_{s,t}\bigr)-k_{t}=0, using a safeguarded Newton-Raphson algorithm to ensure fast convergence to a feasible solution (Ypma, 1995).22 2 The optimization procedure is shown in Alg. 3. We further propose two empirically effective improvements to budget allocation that still respect the global budget KK: a one-time prefix-debt offset δinit​(x)\delta_{\mathrm{init}}(x), and an adaptive rule for defining the stepwise budget ktk_{t}.

3.3 Prefix debt δinit​(x)\delta_{\mathrm{init}}(x)

Not all input prefixes are equally likely to elicit regurgitated continuations. A generic prompt poses little risk, whereas the opening hook of a famous novel may statistically prime the model to output memorized text. We propose to exploit this early signal by offsetting the global KK budget with some context-dependent debt, δinit​(x)\delta_{\mathrm{init}}(x), reflecting the intuition that a risky prompt xx has already pre-spent some of its safety margin by the start of generation. By initializing the banked budget with a negative offset, the available per-step budget is effectively zero in early steps (i.e., we clamp negative ktk_{t} to 0). Thus, our conservative approach is more likely to sample exclusively from psp_{s} in early steps for memorization-triggering prompts.

Inspired by pretraining data detection (Shi et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2025a), we focus on the largest log-likelihood ratios (LLRs) in the prefix. Intuitively, extremely positive LLR outliers mark tokens for which prp_{r} and psp_{s} disagree strongly, suggesting higher memorization likelihood. Let x=(x0,x1,…,xL−1)x{=}(x_{0},x_{1},\ldots,x_{L-1}) be a prefix sequence of length L>1L{>}1. For each position i∈{1,…,L−1}i\in\{1,\ldots,L-1\}, define the pointwise LLR as ℓi​(x):=log⁡pr​(xi∣x<i)ps​(xi∣x<i)\ell_{i}(x):=\log\frac{p_{r}(x_{i}\mid x_{<i})}{p_{s}(x_{i}\mid x_{<i})}. Let [z]+:=max⁡(z,0)[z]_{+}:=\max(z,0) denote the positive part of zz, and let ℐn​(x)\mathcal{I}_{n}(x) be the index set of the nn largest values among {[ℓi​(x)]+}i=1L−1\{[\ell_{i}(x)]_{+}\}_{i=1}^{L-1} (ties broken arbitrarily; if L−1<nL-1{<}n, take all indices). The prefix debt is

δinit​(x):=1max⁡{1,|ℐn​(x)|}​∑i∈ℐn​(x)[ℓi​(x)]+.\displaystyle\delta_{\mathrm{init}}(x):=\frac{1}{\max\{1,|\mathcal{I}_{n}(x)|\}}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{I}_{n}(x)}[\ell_{i}(x)]_{+}. (6)

δinit​(x)\delta_{\mathrm{init}}(x) acts as a one-time reduction of the global budget. As δinit​(x)≥0\delta_{\mathrm{init}}(x)\geq 0 by construction, K−δinit​(x)≤KK-\delta_{\mathrm{init}}(x)\leq K, ensuring that the safety guarantee is preserved (and typically tightened) regardless of the prompt’s content.33 3 We sketch out the prefix debt calculation in Alg. 2.

3.4 An adaptive budgeting strategy

While setting a constant local cap kt≡kk_{t}\equiv k satisfies the global safety condition whenever k​Tmax≤Kk\,T_{\max}\leq K (Corollary 3.2), this naive allocation is often overly conservative. The constraint DK​L(pt∗∥ps)≤kD_{KL}(p_{t}^{*}\,\|\,p_{s})\leq k applies the same allowance at every step and cannot bank unused budget from “easy” steps (i.e., where the models naturally agree, and pt∗p_{t}^{*} is already close to psp_{s}) for later steps. We therefore propose an adaptive budget parameterized by a base rate kk (the knob we sweep) that tracks realized spend and rolls unused budget forward. For shorthand, denote pi∗:=pi∗(⋅|y<i,x)p_{i}^{*}:=p_{i}^{*}(\cdot|y_{<i},x) for timestep ii, and analogously for ps,ip_{s,i}.

Proposition 3.4 (Global safety of adaptive banking).

Let KK be the global safety budget for a sequence up to length TmaxT_{\max}, and let k≔K/Tmaxk\coloneqq K/T_{\max}. Set ai≔DK​L(pi∗∥ps,i)a_{i}\coloneqq D_{KL}\!\bigl(p_{i}^{*}\,\|\,p_{s,i}\bigr) (the actual KL expenditure at each step ii). If, at each decoding step t<Tmaxt<T_{\max}, the per-step adaptive budget ktk_{t} is defined as

kt\displaystyle k_{t} ≔max⁡(0,(t+1)​k−∑i=0t−1ai−δinit​(x)),\displaystyle\coloneqq\max\left(0,(t+1)k-\sum_{i=0}^{t-1}a_{i}-\delta_{\mathrm{init}}(x)\right), (7)

where δinit​(x)≥0\delta_{\mathrm{init}}(x)\geq 0 is some initial budget adjustment for the input prefix xx, then the resulting autoregressive sequence distribution p∗​(y<T|x)=∏t=0T−1pt∗​(yt|y<t,x)p^{*}(y_{<T}|x)=\prod_{t=0}^{T-1}p_{t}^{*}(y_{t}|y_{<t},x) satisfies DK​L(p∗∥ps)≤K−δinit(x)≤KD_{KL}(p^{*}\,\|\,p_{s})\leq K-\delta_{\mathrm{init}}(x)\leq K for any T≤TmaxT\leq T_{\max}.

3.5 Putting Anchored Decoding together

Our complete method (Alg. 1) solves for a fused distribution of the form in Sec. 3.2 at every decoding step. We treat kk as the user-set nominal per-step allotment; for a horizon TmaxT_{\max}, we set the corresponding global budget to K≔k​TmaxK\coloneqq k\,T_{\max} (satisfying Corollary 3.2). The prefix debt δinit​(x)\delta_{\mathrm{init}}(x) (Sec. 3.3) is then applied as a conservative offset, yielding an effective budget K−δinit​(x)K-\delta_{\mathrm{init}}(x). This remaining budget is allocated over the course of decoding, via the adaptive budgeting rule defined in Sec. 3.4. Consequently, Anchored Decoding satisfies the global KK-NAF guarantee for horizon TmaxT_{\max}, while allowing for a tunable per-step allotment kk and the debt window nn.

3.6 AnchoredByte Decoding

Anchored Decoding requires prp_{r} and psp_{s} to share the same vocabulary space, which substantially restricts the set of feasible model pairs. Many safe models psp_{s} (e.g., Comma 7B) use bespoke tokenizers to ensure permissive data usage throughout the language modeling pipeline, making direct token-level fusion with popular model families (e.g., Llama 3) incompatible. This motivates AnchoredByte Decoding, a byte-level version of our method that supports cross-tokenizer compatibility, and retains the weaker assumption that prp_{r} and psp_{s} have Byte Pair Encoding (BPE) (Gage, 1994; Sennrich et al., 2016) tokenizers that induce a mapping from tokens to UTF-8 byte strings.

Defining the byte probability space.

We treat the decoding process as a sequence of byte-level transitions 𝐛=(b0,b1,…,bB−1)\mathbf{b}=(b_{0},b_{1},...,b_{B-1}) for B≤BmaxB\leq B_{\max} using the ByteSampler (Hayase et al., 2025) framework. At each step tt, ByteSampler induces a next-byte distribution over ℬ={0​x​00,…,0​x​F​F}\mathcal{B}=\{0\textrm{x}00,...,0\textrm{x}FF\} by marginalizing the model’s token distribution over all valid tokenizations consistent with the current byte prefix b<tb_{<t}. The probability of a byte bb is obtained by summing the probabilities of valid token continuations whose decoded strings have bb as the next byte, where validity is determined by the model’s tokenizer state for 𝐛<t\mathbf{b}_{<t}. Hayase et al. (2025) implement this marginalization using a Valid Covering Tree traversal, which efficiently produces an exact next-byte distribution induced by the underlying token-level model and tokenizer.

AnchoredByte Decoding satisfies KK-NAF.

AnchoredByte Decoding solves an analogous optimization to Eq. 4 under a similar prefix debt calculation to Eq. 6 and budgeting rule to Eq. 7. The only change when moving to the byte level is that we now operate over the byte space ℬ\mathcal{B} instead of 𝒱\mathcal{V}, and use the induced byte-level distributions of prp_{r} and psp_{s}. Thus, AnchoredByte Decoding remains KK-NAF compliant for K=k​BmaxK=kB_{\max}, where BmaxB_{\max} is the maximum number of generated bytes.44 4 Please see Sec. B.2 for byte-level decoding details. With modern BPE tokenization, one token corresponds to approximately 4 bytes in English (OpenAI, 2022; Pagnoni et al., 2025). This results in more decoding steps for the same semantic length, so we set Bmax≈4​TmaxB_{\max}\approx 4T_{\max}.

3.7 Evaluation metrics

As the determination of copyright infringement is inherently contextual, we measure copyright risk and utility using long-form metrics that holistically score generations.55 5 We provide more evaluation details in App. D.

Copyright infringement.

We consider real copyright risk and evaluate on snippets from Books, a domain of 16 novels taken from CopyBench (Chen et al., 2024) that are currently protected under U.S. copyright law, and are identified as likely to have been memorized by LLMs (Chang et al., 2023; Shi et al., 2024). Following Chen et al. (2024); Wei et al. (2024), we employ the following six metrics (denoted as ℳ\mathcal{M}): ROUGE-1 and ROUGE-L (Lin, 2004) above a set threshold τ=0.4\tau=0.4, MinHash similarity (Broder, 1997), and word-level Accumulated Common Substring (ACS) measure near duplicate copying, while word-level and character-level Longest Common Substring (LCS) measure the extent of exact match.66 6 We also provide non-literal copying experiments in Sec. E.3.

4 Experiments

We assign equal weight to each metric m∈ℳm\in\mathcal{M} and aggregate them into a single normalized copying reduction (NCR) score: formally, let mrm_{r} and msm_{s} denote the metric values for prp_{r} and psp_{s}, respectively. For a given setting with metric value mm, we define its NCR to be mr−mmr−ms\frac{m_{r}-m}{m_{r}-m_{s}}.

NCR quantifies the fraction of the performance gap between prp_{r} and psp_{s} that is closed by the setting. Crucially, we treat psp_{s} as the gold standard for safety rather than aiming for a metric value of zero. Since any non-infringing natural language model may exhibit non-zero baseline overlap due to common linguistic structures, psp_{s} approximates the lower bound of incidental copying achievable without sacrificing fluency. We report the final aggregate result as the average of NCR values across all 6 metrics in ℳ\mathcal{M}.

Finally, we define a high-protection regime as a threshold where the NCR is at least 75%75\%. While the optimal safety threshold is often task-specific, practical deployment typically requires a substantial reduction in copying risk, not marginal improvements. We thus choose this point to isolate regimes where the mitigation effect size is dominant.

Utility.

We consider two types of general utility: fluency and factuality. Fluency measures how natural and well-formed the output reads as; we follow Chen et al. (2024) and evaluate the quality of Books continuations using Prometheus-v2 (Kim et al., 2024), an LLM-as-a-judge (Zheng et al., 2023) that scores output along a five-point rubric (5 being the highest). Factuality is a property that should be preserved, as U.S. copyright law only protects the original expression of factual knowledge, but not facts themselves (Feist Publications, Inc. v. Rural Telephone Service Co., Inc., ).

Consequently, we evaluate long-form factuality on Bios, a collection of biography generation prompts used by FActScore (Min et al., 2023). FActScore is a fine-grained metric that decomposes each output into a set of atomic, verifiable claims (Song et al., 2024), and fact-checks each claim independently against retrieved web search snippets. We report the average claim precision—the fraction of unique supported claims.

4.1 Inference-time baselines

We summarize the mitigation baselines used in our experiments. We defer a broader discussion to Sec. A.2, and provide implementation details in Sec. D.2.

Single-model decoding baselines.

In System, we prepend a system prompt that instructs LMs to refrain from outputting copyrighted material (Chen et al., 2024; The Mosaic Research Team, 2024; Wei et al., 2024; Aerni et al., 2025). MemFree (Ippolito et al., 2023) is a decoding method that blocks exact nn-gram regurgitation by rejecting any next token that would complete an nn-gram from a reference-derived blocklist; we sweep n∈{3,5,7,9,10}n\in\{3,5,7,9,10\}. Reversed Context Aware Decoding (Wei et al., 2024), or RCAD, contrasts logits with and without a blocklisted context and produces a next-token distribution that downweights tokens favored by context (modulated using α\alpha); we sweep α∈{0.1,0.25,0.5,0.75,1.0}\alpha\in\{0.1,0.25,0.5,0.75,1.0\}. We apply these baselines to prp_{r}, and for MemFree and RCAD, we simulate realistic deployment and construct the context blocklist by retrieving the top-1 passage from an in-domain datastore (e.g., Books3 for Books, and Wikipedia for Bios).

Joint-model decoding baselines.

We consider CP-Fuse (Abad et al., 2025), a KK-NAF-inspired fusion method that selects a next-token distribution by balancing proximity to two LMs of equal utility. CP-Fuse assumes the copyrighted portions of the training data can be cleanly separated across the two models (i.e., disjoint data shards). It solves for a per-step fused distribution by minimizing the maximum KL divergence across the model pair. TokenSwap (Prashant et al., 2025) constructs a hybrid next-token distribution by swapping a manually defined set of common tokens (e.g., function words) from a small model onto a large model’s distribution, while leaving all other token probabilities unchanged. For baseline consistency, we instantiate CP-Fuse and TokenSwap using our asymmetric pair (pr,ps)(p_{r},p_{s}).

4.2 Model pairs

Following prior memorization work (Carlini et al., 2021; Carlini et al., 2023; Abad et al., 2025; Prashant et al., 2025), we instantiate psp_{s} and prp_{r} as base (non-instruction-tuned) LMs to isolate memorization effects in the underlying next-token distributions. For risky models prp_{r}, we choose Llama 3.1 70B (Grattafiori et al., 2024), Qwen 2.5 72B (Qwen Team, 2024), and Llama 4 Scout 17Bx16E (Meta AI, 2025), which exhibit measurable verbatim reproduction in our copying evaluations. We select capable safe models psp_{s} that are trained on the Common Pile (Kandpal et al., 2025). To ensure tokenizer compatibility with Llama 3.1, we pre-train our own TinyComma 1.8B on the 169.5B tokens from the Common Pile, which outperforms other size-matched psp_{s} (Min et al., 2024; Bommarito II et al., 2025; Langlais et al., 2025) on general language understanding tasks.77 7 In Sec. C.1, we provide TinyComma 1.8B pre-training details and show benchmarking results for various psp_{s} candidates on standard natural language tasks. We also use the larger and more performant Comma 7B (Kandpal et al., 2025), which was trained for 2T tokens and has a custom tokenizer. Our selection of ps,prp_{s},p_{r} leads to six model pairs, of which only TinyComma 1.8B and Llama 3.1 70B are tokenizer-matched. We apply Anchored Decoding to that pair, and AnchoredByte Decoding to all others.

4.3 Hyperparameters

We sweep our methods across a range of kk: {0.1,0.5,1,1.5,2,3,4,5,10,15,20}\{0.1,0.5,1,1.5,2,3,4,5,10,15,20\}. We set Tmax=200T_{\max}{=}200 and Bmax=800B_{\max}{=}800 bytes, and n=5n{=}5 as the debt window.88 8 We find Anchored Decoding to be largely insensitive to the choice of nn and provide more details in Sec. C.3.

5 Results

5.1 Risk–utility trade-offs

Fig. 1(b) and Fig. 2 show trade-off curves among mitigation baselines for (token-level) Anchored and (byte-level) AnchoredByte Decoding, respectively. 99 9 Sec. D.6 shows qualitative examples. The results are striking: at both granularities, our methods trace the Pareto frontier (upper-right zone) across all model pairs, with statistical significance over 3 random seeds. Table 1 highlights the best utility achieved by each method among configurations that meet the high-protection operating point (i.e., NCR≥75%{\geq}75\%). Our methods consistently yield the strongest utility within this region. For example, under the token-level pair {TinyComma 1.8B, Llama 3.1 70B}, Anchored Decoding achieves 0.53 in factuality and 4.02 in fluency, surpassing the strongest two-model baseline that meets the threshold (TokenSwap: 0.44 / 3.77) and the single-model baselines that do (e.g., RCAD: 0.37 / 3.38; MemFree: 0.37 / 3.18). Similar trends persist at the byte level: for {Comma 7B, Llama 3.1 70B}, AnchoredByte Decoding achieves 0.52 / 4.23, exceeding CP-Fuse (0.23 / 3.75), TokenSwap (0.49 / 3.89), and RCAD (0.46 / 3.46).

Among pointwise baselines, System shows high utility but scarcely achieves copying reduction (and for pr=p_{r}{=}Qwen 2.5 72B, is even slightly worse than prp_{r}). While CP-Fuse and TokenSwap achieve high NCR and mostly fall within the high-protection operating point, they also experience worse utility. Among parametric baselines, both RCAD and MemFree tend to operate well below the high-protection operating point; even when they do surpass the threshold, it comes at a substantial utility cost.

5.2 Anchored Decoding ablations

We choose the token-level pair {TinyComma 1.8B, Llama 3.1 70B} to study three ablation axes: (i) optimization objective, (ii) prefix debt, and (iii) budgeting strategy.

Optimization objective.

First, in our Anchored Decoding∞\infty setting, we take the ∞\infty-Rényi  divergence function as our divergence metric (Rényi, 1961), which supplies a worst-case guarantee instead of an average-case one, and is commonly employed in sensitive machine learning applications such as differential privacy (Dwork, 2006; Mironov, 2017), where the objective is to bound the maximum possible information leakage from any single observation. The alternative derivation of Anchored Decoding with ∞\infty-Rényi divergence leads to an analytical, closed-form solution. We show that this instantiation satisfies KK-NAF in Sec. B.3. In NoOpt, we ablate the optimization and retain the budget and prefix debt; at each step, we sample from prp_{r} if DK​L​(pr∣ps)≤ktD_{KL}(p_{r}\mid p_{s})\leq k_{t}, and psp_{s}, otherwise. Finally, in ColdStart, we use the per-step cap kk and sample only from psp_{s} for the first k×10k\times 10 steps, after which we sample from prp_{r}.

Prefix debt δinit​(x)\delta_{\mathrm{init}}(x).

We ablate the prefix debt by removing it entirely (NoDebt). In AvgDebt, we experiment with treat δinit​(x)\delta_{\mathrm{init}}(x){} as an aggregate statistic by averaging over all prefix LLRs instead of taking the top-nn largest values.

Budget allocation.

We explore alternative budget allocation schemes: in Fixed, we assign a per-step, constant budget kk, with no rollover of unused budget across timesteps. In Global, we allocate the full budget K=k​TmaxK=kT_{\max} upfront and enforce only a cumulative constraint: we decode from prp_{r} until the running KL spend from psp_{s} reaches KK, then switch to sampling from psp_{s} for the rest of generation.

Ablation results.

Fig. 3 shows ablation trade-off plots. For (1) Optimization Objective, Anchored Decoding is strictly more Pareto-optimal than both NoOpt and ColdStart ablations. Our ∞\infty-Rényi version, Anchored Decoding∞\infty, attains a better fluency trade-off but worse factuality than our KL-based formulation, and serves as a strong, principled alternative for practitioners.

For (ii) Prefix Debt, replacing our top-nn LLR aggregation with an average over all prefix LLRs (AvgDebt) yields a consistently worse trade-off, underscoring our treatment of prefix debt as a tail statistic. Removing the prefix debt altogether (NoDebt) further degrades the curve. And for (iii) Budgeting Strategy, Anchored Decoding’s adaptive budget—which accounts for realized spend in prior steps—leads to a strictly better trade-off than either a constant cap (Fixed) or a holistic lump-sum budget (Global).

5.3 Efficiency

A practical consideration for safety-constrained decoding is inference-time overhead. Table 2 reports time to first token (TTFT), throughput slowdown relative to prp_{r} (TPS Ratio), and FLOPs estimate for the token-level pair {TinyComma 1.8B, Llama 3.1 70B}, computed as 2​(Nr+Ns)2(N_{r}+N_{s}), where NrN_{r}, NsN_{s} are parameter counts for prp_{r}, psp_{s}, respectively (see Sec. D.5 for formal derivations).1010 10 We provide byte-level wall-clock measurements in Sec. D.5. We run all settings on 2 140 GiB NVIDIA H200s. As expected for joint-model decoding, Anchored Decoding incurs a modest throughput overhead, operating ≈1.1×\approx 1.1\times slower than standalone prp_{r} decoding. While the additional forward pass with psp_{s} increases arithmetic compute by only ≈2.6%\approx 2.6\% (from 143.6 to 140 GFLOPs/token), the observed wall-clock slowdown is consistent with bandwidth- and synchronization-bound overheads from logit fusion. All methods are more efficient than RCAD, which requires two forward passes with prp_{r}.

6 Analysis

We perform targeted experiments to motivate the design choices behind Anchored Decoding (Sec. 6.1). We first find that per-step KL(pr∥ps)\mathrm{KL}(p_{r}\,\|\,p_{s}) serves as a reliable proxy for identifying memorization by prp_{r} but not psp_{s} (Sec. 6.2). Next, we show that copying risk is front-loaded in early generation, motivating the prefix debt (Sec. 6.3).

6.1 Experimental Setting

We conduct our analyses at token and byte granularities using the representative model pair {ps=TinyComma 1.8B,pr=Llama 3.1 70B}\{p_{s}=\text{TinyComma 1.8B{}},\;p_{r}=\text{Llama 3.1 70B}\} on three prompt domains (180 prefixes each).

Copyright contains copyright-protected book excerpts from Books. Factual consists of biography generation prompts from FActScore. A potential confound is that these two prompt sets differ in domain and style, so any diagnostic separation may reflect distributional shift. As a control, we introduce a Creative domain by scraping original story prompts from Reddit’s r/WritingPrompts community (from 2024–2025, after Llama 3.1’s training cutoff). Creative is roughly in-distribution to Copyright; Table 15 shows qualitative examples. Neither LM should have memorized any Creative or Factual prompts, but prp_{r} has likely memorized some Copyright prompts.

6.2 KL is a Useful Memorization Diagnostic

We test whether the per-step divergence between risky and safe models can meaningfully separate copyright-sensitive prefixes from benign ones. Namely, for each prefix xx, we sample a continuation from prp_{r} for T=50T{=}50 tokens (or B=200B{=}200 bytes), and compute DK​L(pr(⋅∣y<t,x)∥ps(⋅∣y<t,x))D_{KL}\!\left(p_{r}(\cdot\mid y_{<t},x)\,\|\,p_{s}(\cdot\mid y_{<t},x)\right) at each decoding step tt of the rollout. When prp_{r} follows a memorized passage that psp_{s} has not learned, then prp_{r}’s next-token distribution becomes sharply peaked on a specific continuation that psp_{s} considers unlikely. This mismatch yields consistently large per-step DK​L(pr∥ps)D_{KL}(p_{r}\|p_{s}) values across decoding steps.

Consistent with this intuition, the top row of Fig. 4 shows that Copyright prefixes are systematically right-shifted relative to Creative and Factual ones. This difference is most pronounced in the extreme right tail (bottom row): we plot the empirical CCDF of per-step DK​L​(pr|ps)D_{KL}(p_{r}|p_{s}) for x≥q90(pooled)x\geq q_{90}^{(\mathrm{pooled})}, where q90(pooled)q_{90}^{(\mathrm{pooled})} is the pooled 90th percentile (shared cutoff per panel). Under this common threshold, the Copyright domain has the largest tail mass—i.e., for any large xx, it has the highest fraction of steps with DK​L(pr∥ps)≥xD_{KL}(p_{r}\|p_{s})\geq x—while Creative and Factual place little mass on such extreme deviations. These results motivate using per-step KL(pr∥ps)\mathrm{KL}(p_{r}\|p_{s}) to detect when generation is in a copyright-sensitive regime.

6.3 Copying Risk is Front-loaded in Early Generation

Our second finding is that the generation of tokens favored by prp_{r} and not psp_{s} is not uniformly distributed over a continuation: copying events tend to occur early in generation.

To quantify this positional bias, we compute two surface-copying metrics—the longest common substring (LCS) and the average common substring (ACS)—and, for each continuation from a Copyright prompt, we record the start position of the first matched substring (i.e., where copyright infringement begins). We report two regimes: (i) any overlap (ACS, LCS >0>0) and (ii) substantial overlap (ACS, LCS ≥5\geq 5).

As Fig. 5 shows, overlap events concentrate heavily at the beginning and drop sharply with generation across both regimes. This front-loading behavior motivates a stronger copyright-mitigation intervention in early decoding steps, which we operationalize by intentionally forcing greater reliance on psp_{s} via the prefix debt. δinit​(x)\delta_{\mathrm{init}}(x) treats the prompt as a memorization prior and debits the global budget KK in proportion to how strongly the prefix favors prp_{r} over psp_{s}. Concretely, we estimate δinit​(x)\delta_{\mathrm{init}}(x) from the upper tail of prefix log-likelihood ratios (average of the top-nn positive LLRs), so that a small number of outlier prompt tokens (or bytes) can trigger greater reliance on psp_{s}.

Copyright prefixes display heavier right tails in prefix LLRs than either Copyright or Factual prefixes, persisting into extreme quantiles (e.g., the 99.599.5 percentile) (Fig. 6). When we directly examine prefix debt values (e.g., the average of the top-5 largest positive prefix LLRs), this tail behavior translates into a similar right-shifted distribution for Copyright. These patterns justify a “cold start” only when prefixes exhibit evidence of asymmetric memorization.

7 Discussion

Anchored Decoding confers several desirable properties. The first is flexibility: by providing a controllable sequence-level safety budget KK, our strategy allows practitioners to specify a desired risk threshold that retains formal guarantees. Second, Anchored Decoding is practical, as it requires neither re-training nor access to the original pre-training data at inference time. This allows for the immediate and retroactive safe-guarding of high-utility models with considerable infringement leakage. Moreover, through AnchoredByte Decoding, we demonstrate that our strategy is tokenizer-agnostic and works effectively across model pairs with mismatched vocabularies. Finally, we show that Anchored Decoding yields a strong risk–utility trade-off, leveraging the observation that the contrast between risky and safe models provides a signal for when generation is likely in a copyrighted regime.

While Sec. A.3 discusses future directions in greater detail, we note that Anchored Decoding extends beyond copyright mitigation in LMs. The same mechanism applies wherever a high-capability model must be bounded by a trusted anchor distribution, for example, to reduce sensitive-attribute leakage, enforce domain or policy restrictions for safety, or align generation with licensed corpora in enterprise settings. Ultimately, our results motivate a reference-anchored decoding paradigm in which practitioners choose the reference model to match the compliance target of interest.

8 Impact Statement

Our work addresses a critical and timely challenge at the intersection of generative AI and intellectual property, amid a recent series of ongoing high-profile litigation and a rapidly evolving legal landscape.

LMs are trained on large-scale, web-scraped corpora that may include copyright-protected material, which precipitates several harms. On the creator side, model outputs that exhibit substantial similarity to protected training examples may infringe on intellectual property rights and erode the market value of original works (Henderson et al., 2023). These issues are compounded by the lack of systematic mechanisms for creator consent (Longpre et al., 2024) or compensation (Baack et al., 2025; Kandpal & Raffel, 2025). On the developer side, as the applicability of the U.S. fair use doctrine (United States Code, 2024) to model training remains unsettled, LM memorization and reproduction may expose developers to significant liability risk. Anchored Decoding targets these concerns as a post-hoc technical mitigation strategy that constrains generation toward a trusted reference distribution at inference time, reducing verbatim reproduction of protected documents and promoting more transformative outputs. And in order to more closely bridge theory and deployment, we design Anchored Decoding to be universally compatible with modern LMs. When tokenizers are aligned, we may operate at the token level; otherwise, our byte-level integration removes the shared-vocabulary requirement and supports LM pairs with mismatched tokenizers.

Nevertheless, Anchored Decoding is not a silver bullet; it cannot completely eliminate infringement risk, and our guarantees and empirical results apply only under the assumptions and evaluation protocol of our study. In light of ongoing legal and policy discourse surrounding generative AI, no legal conclusions ought to be inferred from this work. Ultimately, we view our contribution as complementary to other safeguards and as one part of a broader toolbox for responsible deployment.

Appendix A General Information

A.1 Released artifacts

We release the following artifacts for reproducibility and future development:

Codebase jacqueline-he/anchored-decoding
TinyComma 1.8B jacquelinehe/tinycomma-1.8b-llama3-tokenizer

A.2 Related Work

Interventions against LM copyright infringement.

Recently proposed strategies have sought to minimize copyright risk at all stages of the language modeling pipeline. Pre-training efforts include training only on public domain and openly licensed texts (Min et al., 2024; Kandpal et al., 2025), or modifying the next-token prediction objective to selectively mask pre-training spans either randomly (Hans et al., 2024) or in a targeted manner (Wang et al., 2025a) to discourage their exact reproduction. A separate line of work applies a secondary post-hoc learning stage to an already pre-trained model, in order to excise undesirable knowledge (i.e., model unlearning (Maini et al., 2024; Yao et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2024; Russinovich & Salem, 2025)) or align with user intent to suppress the unintentional regurgitation of training data (Chen et al., 2025). Finally, some methods operate post-generation by identifying infringing spans—either via efficient Bloom filters applied to pre-training corpora (Zhang et al., 2025b) or via multi-agent web searches (Liu et al., 2024)—before rewriting them into non-offending versions using LLMs.

Our approach centers on the decoding stage, motivated by the observation that training or re-training frontier LLMs is an expensive endeavor; likewise, multi-agent pipelines incur nontrivial inference overhead and do not change the underlying generative process. However, we view Anchored Decoding as orthogonal to pre-training, post-training, and post-generation procedures, and leave their integration to future work.

While many techniques are heuristic, Vyas et al. (2023) formalizes the theoretical notion of provable copyright protection at inference time via KK-Near Access Freeness, which forms the groundwork to Anchored Decoding. Anchored Decoding shares theoretical similarities to CP-Fuse (Abad et al., 2025), which to our knowledge is the only other KK-NAF–inspired algorithm, but we note a few differences. First, CP-Fuse assumes that copyright-infringing datapoints are not known a priori, and thus requires an LM pair trained on discrete data shards, where no single datum appears in both models’ training sets. This restriction is quite unrealistic for off-the-shelf, production-grade LLMs, whose data provenance is often unknown or undisclosed. In contrast, Anchored Decoding implicitly assumes that the set of copyright-infringing data is known and may be in prp_{r}, but not psp_{s}. Second, CP-Fuse is a pointwise baseline and does not allow the user to specify a preferred risk tolerance; in our experiments, this manifests as degraded utility. On the other hand, Anchored Decoding exposes a control knob that allows for tuning of the risk-utility trade-off curve.

Two-model decoding methods.

Anchored Decoding belongs to a proliferative body of literature that proposes to decode using asymmetric model pairs. One category focuses on expert-guided generation via model arithmetic (Liu et al., 2021; Li et al., 2023a), which involves amplifying a high-capability “expert” model by downweighting undesirable characteristics from an “amateur” model. Another class employs a drafter-verifier framework to accelerate inference, and notably includes speculative decoding (Chen et al., 2023; Leviathan et al., 2023; Li et al., 2024), in which a lightweight draft model proposes candidates for a larger model to verify. Our approach employs a dual-model structure with a different objective: rather than optimizing purely for downstream performance or efficiency, Anchored Decoding seeks to generate text with less copyright infringement in a utility-preserving manner.

Closest to Anchored Decoding is TokenSwap (Prashant et al., 2025), which operates with a mismatched-size model pair and leverages the empirical observation that smaller models tend to memorize less than the larger one (Kandpal et al., 2023). This heuristic is rather coarse: both models can still reproduce protected text, especially for spans that appear frequently in pre-training corpora. Moreover, TokenSwap relies on swapping a predefined list of common English tokens (largely function/grammar tokens), which limits its portability across languages and cannot address copying events that do not pass through the chosen token set. Anchored Decoding bypasses both limitations through (i) an explicit safe–risky model pairing (rather than relying on model size as a proxy for memorization) and (ii) distribution-level fusion that enforces a divergence budget to the safe model at every decoding step.

Finally, many two-model decoding methods assume a shared tokenization vocabulary. We remove this bottleneck by adapting our method (and relevant baselines) to operate via ByteSampler (Hayase et al., 2025), and show that the same algorithms at the byte level still ensure the strong mitigation of training data reproduction. Many approximate methods have been proposed to overcome mismatching vocabularies in model ensembles, such as using beam search as a scoring function (Kasai et al., 2022) or using a mapping based on model features (Huang et al., 2024); we opted for bytewise sampling under ByteSampler as it is gives exactly the same distributions of output text (Hayase et al., 2025). Beyond copyright reduction, byte-level decoding suggests a general route for making two-model decoding practical in cross-tokenizer settings.

A.3 Limitations and Future Work

Probabilistic risk. To begin, Anchored Decoding does not fully eliminate the possibility of generating protected spans. Our method is a sampling strategy instead of a discrete filtering or blocking mechanism. It inherently inherits the baseline risk profile of the safe model, psp_{s}. While the probability of psp_{s} reproducing a sequence it was not exposed to during training is typically very small, it remains strictly non-zero. Under the KK-NAF framework, we only guarantee that the risk of an infringing generation is comparable to the safe baseline within a bounded, controllable distance.

Local approximation. Additionally, while Anchored Decoding solves a local optimization at each step for computational tractability, this sequential approximation may not represent the global optimum of the sequence-level constrained objective. This is a necessary trade-off for efficient autoregressive decoding.

Asymmetric memorization as an imperfect proxy. Our framework treats asymmetric memorization—what prp_{r} has memorized, but psp_{s} has not, via large deviations in metrics such as per-step KL or prefix LLR—as a proxy indicator of elevated copying risk. However, these signals are not unique to copyright: they can also arise when the risky model contains useful long-tail knowledge that the safe model lacks. Because we intentionally chose larger models as prp_{r}, which naturally memorize a broader tail spectrum of facts than the smaller models we select as psp_{s}, our divergence constraints may inadvertently suppress rare, non-copyrighted factual information. Note that this phenomenon is highly model-pair dependent, and should be mitigated when the safe reference is closer in capability to the risky baseline.

Data provenance and latent leakage.

Another limitation is that the efficacy of Anchored Decoding relies on the a priori identification of model pairs with known data provenance. Specifically, the safe model psp_{s} must be verified as having been trained exclusively on copyright-free or openly licensed data. There is also an inherent risk of latent copyright leakage: protected fragments (e.g., famous literary quotes) may still permeate ostensibly open-licensed data (e.g., within blog posts or public forums). In such cases, psp_{s} may exhibit a baseline propensity to reproduce such protected sequences, a risk that Anchored Decoding can bound but not entirely eliminate.

Future directions.

Beyond copyrighted text, we believe that Anchored Decoding is applicable wherever a high-capability, high-risk generator must be bounded by a trusted reference distribution. Our approach is agnostic to tokenizer, modality, and domain. Our byte-level experiments demonstrate that decoding effects are persistent regardless of the tokenization scheme, and we encourage future two-model decoding baselines to adopt byte-level evaluations to ensure broader architectural compatibility. One promising direction is to extend our framework to generative AI technologies beyond LLMs, e.g., image or video generation, where the risk of memorizing protected artistic styles or iconic visual frames presents similar copyright challenges (He et al., 2025; Moayeri et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025b). For instance, diffusion models from the CommonCanvas suite—trained on Creative Commons–licensed images—are promising permissively trained candidates for psp_{s} (Gokaslan et al., 2023). Another direction is the application of Anchored Decoding to other domains, e.g., policy compliance, code safety, or privacy redaction, to suppress the leakage of sensitive information in a focused manner while retaining general capabilities.

Further, for each token yt∈𝒱y_{t}\in\mathcal{V}, we can differentiate ℒ\mathcal{L} with respect to p⁡(yt)p(y_{t}) and set to zero, leading to

∂ℒ∂p⁡(yt)=log⁡p⁡(yt)pr​(yt)+1+λ⁡(log⁡p⁡(yt)ps​(yt)+1)+α=0.\displaystyle\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial p(y_{t})}=\log\frac{p(y_{t})}{p_{r}(y_{t})}+1+\lambda\!\left(\log\frac{p(y_{t})}{p_{s}(y_{t})}+1\right)+\alpha=0. (12)

Rearranging terms to isolate log⁡p⁡(yt)\log p(y_{t}), we have:

(1+λ)​log⁡p⁡(yt)\displaystyle(1+\lambda)\log p(y_{t}) =log⁡pr​(yt)+λ​log⁡ps​(yt)−(1+λ+α).\displaystyle=\log p_{r}(y_{t})+\lambda\log p_{s}(y_{t})-(1+\lambda+\alpha). (13)

Dividing by (1+λ)(1+\lambda) and exponentiating both sides:

p⁡(yt)\displaystyle p(y_{t}) =exp⁡(log⁡pr​(yt)+λ​log⁡ps​(yt)1+λ)⋅exp⁡(−1+λ+α1+λ)\displaystyle=\exp\left(\frac{\log p_{r}(y_{t})+\lambda\log p_{s}(y_{t})}{1+\lambda}\right)\cdot\exp\left(-\frac{1+\lambda+\alpha}{1+\lambda}\right) (14)
=1Z​pr​(yt)11+λ​ps​(yt)λ1+λ,\displaystyle=\frac{1}{Z}p_{r}(y_{t})^{\frac{1}{1+\lambda}}p_{s}(y_{t})^{\frac{\lambda}{1+\lambda}}, (15)

where Z=exp⁡(1+λ+α1+λ)Z=\exp\left(\frac{1+\lambda+\alpha}{1+\lambda}\right) acts as the normalization constant to satisfy the simplex constraint. ∎

B.1.3 An adaptive banking budget.

See 3.4

Proof.

Fix any T≤TmaxT\leq T_{\max} and any realized trajectory y0:T−1∼p∗(⋅∣x)y_{0:T-1}\sim p^{*}(\cdot\mid x). Let St≔∑i=0taiS_{t}\coloneqq\sum_{i=0}^{t}a_{i} denote the cumulative realized expenditure up to step tt.

St≤max⁡{0,(t+1)​k−δinit​(x)}.\displaystyle S_{t}\;\leq\;\max\{0,\ (t+1)k-\delta_{\mathrm{init}}(x)\}. (16)
Base case (t=0t=0).

By feasibility, a0≤k0=max⁡{0,k−δinit​(x)}a_{0}\leq k_{0}=\max\{0,k-\delta_{\mathrm{init}}(x)\}, hence S0=a0≤max⁡{0,k−δinit​(x)}S_{0}=a_{0}\leq\max\{0,k-\delta_{\mathrm{init}}(x)\}.

Inductive step (t>1t>1).

St\displaystyle S_{t} =St−1+at\displaystyle=S_{t-1}+a_{t} (17)
≤St−1+max⁡{0,(t+1)​k−St−1−δinit​(x)}\displaystyle\leq S_{t-1}+\max\{0,\ (t+1)k-S_{t-1}-\delta_{\mathrm{init}}(x)\} (18)
=max⁡{St−1,(t+1)​k−δinit​(x)}\displaystyle=\max\{S_{t-1},\ (t+1)k-\delta_{\mathrm{init}}(x)\} (19)
≤max⁡{0,(t+1)​k−δinit​(x)},\displaystyle\leq\max\{0,\ (t+1)k-\delta_{\mathrm{init}}(x)\}, (20)

where the last line uses St−1≥0S_{t-1}\geq 0 (since each ai≥0a_{i}\geq 0). This completes the induction.

Applying (16) at t=T−1t=T-1 gives

∑t=0T−1at=ST−1≤max⁡{0,T​k−δinit​(x)}≤max⁡{0,K−δinit​(x)},\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}a_{t}=S_{T-1}\ \leq\ \max\{0,\ Tk-\delta_{\mathrm{init}}(x)\}\ \leq\ \max\{0,\ K-\delta_{\mathrm{init}}(x)\},

DK​L(p∗(y0:T−1∣x)∥ps(y0:T−1∣x))=𝔼y∼p∗[∑t=0T−1at]≤max{0,K−δinit(x)}≤K,D_{KL}(p^{*}(y_{0:T-1}\mid x)\,\|\,p_{s}(y_{0:T-1}\mid x))=\mathbb{E}_{y\sim p^{*}}\left[\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}a_{t}\right]\leq\max\{0,\ K-\delta_{\mathrm{init}}(x)\}\leq K,

B.2 AnchoredByte Decoding

Satisfying KK-NAF with AnchoredByte Decoding.
Remark B.2 (Safety preservation under byte-level decoding).

Let 𝖡𝗒𝗍𝖾⁡(⋅)\mathsf{Byte}(\cdot) denote the operator that maps a token-level LM to the induced autoregressive distribution over UTF-8 bytes by exactly marginalizing token probabilities into a next-byte distribution at each byte prefix (using the ByteSampler abstraction). Define p~s≔𝖡𝗒𝗍𝖾⁡(ps)\tilde{p}_{s}\coloneqq\mathsf{Byte}(p_{s}) and p~r≔𝖡𝗒𝗍𝖾⁡(pr)\tilde{p}_{r}\coloneqq\mathsf{Byte}(p_{r}); notably, this mapping is strictly procedural and requires no auxiliary data, additional models, or further training. The global KK-NAF guarantee applies to the byte transition space through three consistent translations:

  1. 1.

    Byte-level optimization: By the chain rule for KL divergence over discrete autoregressive transitions, if DK​L(p~i∗∥p~s,i)≤kiD_{KL}(\tilde{p}_{i}^{*}\,\|\,\tilde{p}_{s,i})\leq k_{i} at every byte step ii, then

    DK​L(p~∗∥p~s)=𝔼𝐛∼p~∗[∑i=0B−1DK​L(p~i∗∥p~s,i)]≤K−δinit(x~)≤K,D_{KL}(\tilde{p}^{*}\,\|\,\tilde{p}_{s})=\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{b}\sim\tilde{p}^{*}}\left[\sum_{i=0}^{B-1}D_{KL}(\tilde{p}_{i}^{*}\,\|\,\tilde{p}_{s,i})\right]\leq K-\delta_{\mathrm{init}}(\tilde{x})\leq K,

    for some δinit​(x~)≥0\delta_{\mathrm{init}}(\tilde{x})\geq 0.

  2. 2.

    Byte-level banking budget: The adaptive budget kik_{i} at byte-step ii is updated as:

    ki=max(0,(i+1)k−∑j=0i−1DK​L(p~j∗∥p~s,j)−δinit(x~)),k_{i}=\max\left(0,\;(i+1)k-\sum_{j=0}^{i-1}D_{KL}(\tilde{p}_{j}^{*}\,\|\,\tilde{p}_{s,j})-\delta_{\mathrm{init}}(\tilde{x})\right),

    where k=K/Bmaxk=K/B_{\max} is the nominal per-byte allotment.

  3. 3.

    Byte-level prefix debt: The prefix debt δinit​(x~)\delta_{\mathrm{init}}(\tilde{x}) is calculated as the mean of the top-nn LLR spikes across the LL bytes of the prefix byte sequence x~\tilde{x}, ensuring δinit​(x~)≥0\delta_{\mathrm{init}}(\tilde{x})\geq 0.

Thus, the safety guarantee is also applicable in the byte transition space.

By decoding byte-by-byte, AnchoredByte Decoding offers finer-grained control for copyright prediction than token-level Anchored Decoding: enforcing the budget at each byte step can steer the distribution away from a memorized string at the exact character of divergence, rather than at the granularity of multi-byte tokens.

B.3 Anchored Decoding with ∞\infty-Rényi  Divergence

Thus far, the Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence has been our primary vehicle for measuring and constraining distributional deviation. As an expectation-based metric, DK​LD_{KL} supplies an average-case guarantee over the sequence. We primarily retain the KL-based interpretation of Anchored Decoding, as a worst-case criterion is overly restrictive—historically, arbitration of copyright infringement hinges on substantial similarity (e.g., the “total concept and feel” standard in Roth Greeting Cards v. United Card Co. (1970)), rather than the occurrence of a single high-probability token. However, Anchored Decoding∞\infty. However, in the case that one desires worst-case guarantees, then the Rényi divergence of order ∞\infty, 𝒟=D∞\mathcal{D}=D_{\infty} would be more useful. Formally, given discrete probability distributions PP and QQ on the same support, D∞D_{\infty} captures the maximum pointwise log-ratio of probabilites:

D∞(P∥Q)\displaystyle D_{\infty}(P\,\|\,Q) =limα→∞1α−1​log​∑xP​(x)α​Q​(x)1−α=log⁡maxx​P⁡(x)Q⁡(x).\displaystyle=\lim_{\alpha\rightarrow\infty}\frac{1}{\alpha-1}\log\sum_{x}P(x)^{\alpha}Q(x)^{1-\alpha}=\log\max_{x}\frac{P(x)}{Q(x)}. (21)
Global objective.

If we apply Definition 2.1 to our problem, using D∞D_{\infty}, we obtain:

p∗=arg​minp\displaystyle p^{*}=\argmin_{p}\quad D∞(p(⋅∣x)∥pr(⋅∣x))s.t.D∞(p(⋅∣x)∥ps(⋅∣x))≤K,\displaystyle D_{\infty}\big(p(\cdot\mid x)\,\|\,p_{r}(\cdot\mid x)\big)\quad\text{s.t.}\quad D_{\infty}\big(p(\cdot\mid x)\,\|\,p_{s}(\cdot\mid x)\big)\leq K, (22)

which, as a sequence-level objective, is computationally intractable for autoregressive decoding.

Token-level approximation.

Given a input sequence xx and for any output history y<t∼p∗(⋅|x)y_{<t}\sim p^{*}(\cdot|x) generated thus far, the token-level approximation at each step step tt can be written as

pt∗(⋅|y<t,x)\displaystyle p_{t}^{*}(\cdot|y_{<t},x) =arg​minp∈Δ⁡(𝒱)(D∞(p∥pr(⋅∣y<t,x)))\displaystyle=\argmin_{p\in\Delta(\mathcal{V})}\Big(D_{\infty}\big(p\,\|\,p_{r}(\cdot\mid y_{<t},x)\big)\Big)\quad (23)
s.t.D∞(p∥ps(⋅∣y<t,x))≤kt,∑y∈𝒱p(y)=1,p(y)>0∀y∈𝒱.\displaystyle\text{s.t.}\quad D_{\infty}\big(p\,\|\,p_{s}(\cdot\mid y_{<t},x)\big)\leq k_{t},\quad\sum_{y\in\mathcal{V}}p(y)=1,\quad p(y)>0\quad\forall y\in\mathcal{V}.

We show that if the per-step constraints in Eq. 23 hold for all t<Tmaxt<T_{\max} and ∑t=0Tmax−1kt≤K\sum_{t=0}^{T_{\max}-1}k_{t}\leq K, then any TT-length continuation generated by yt∼pt∗(⋅|y<t,x)y_{t}\sim p_{t}^{*}(\cdot|y_{<t},x) for T≤TmaxT\leq T_{\max} is a valid solution to the global sequence-level objective defined in Eq. 22.

Theorem B.3 (Safety of local approximation with 𝒟=D∞\mathcal{D}=D_{\infty}).

Let p∗p^{*} be a sequence-level distribution defined autoregressively by p∗​(y<T|x)=∏t=0T−1pt∗​(yt|y<t,x)p^{*}(y_{<T}|x)=\prod_{t=0}^{T-1}p_{t}^{*}(y_{t}|y_{<t},x). If, for all decoding steps t<Tmaxt<T_{\max}, the conditional distribution pt∗p^{*}_{t} solves Eq. 23 with a per-step budget kt≥0k_{t}\geq 0 such that ∑t=0Tmax−1kt≤K\sum_{t=0}^{T_{\max}-1}k_{t}\leq K, then p∗p^{*} satisfies the global KK-NAF guarantee in Eq. 22 for all T≤TmaxT\leq T_{\max}.

Proof.

Observe that

D∞(p∗(⋅|x)∥ps(⋅|x))\displaystyle D_{\infty}(p^{*}(\cdot|x)\,\|\,p_{s}(\cdot|x)) =logmaxy0:T−1p∗(y0:T−1|x)ps(y0:T−1|x)\displaystyle=\log\max_{y_{0:T-1}}\frac{p^{*}(y_{0:T-1}|x)}{p_{s}(y_{0:T-1}|x)} (24)
=logmaxy0:T−1∏t=0T−1pt∗​(yt|y<t,x)ps​(yt|y<t,x)(per-token product form)\displaystyle=\log\max_{y_{0:T-1}}\prod_{t=0}^{T-1}\frac{p^{*}_{t}(y_{t}|y_{<t},x)}{p_{s}(y_{t}|y_{<t},x)}\qquad\textrm{(per-token product form)} (25)
=maxy0:T−1∑t=0T−1logpt∗​(yt∣y<t,x)ps​(yt∣y<t,x)(log monotone; log∏=∑log)\displaystyle=\max_{y_{0:T-1}}\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}\log\frac{p_{t}^{*}(y_{t}\mid y_{<t},x)}{p_{s}(y_{t}\mid y_{<t},x)}\qquad(\log\text{ monotone; }\log\prod=\sum\log) (26)
≤maxy0:T−1∑t=0T−1kt≤∑t=0Tmax−1kt≤K.\displaystyle\leq\max_{y_{0:T-1}}\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}k_{t}\leq\sum_{t=0}^{T_{\max}-1}k_{t}\leq K. (27)

The transition from Eq. 26 to Eq. 27 holds because our local optimization ensures that for any history y<ty_{<t}, the maximum log-ratio never exceeds ktk_{t}. Thus, the global KK-NAF condition is satisfied. ∎

We next show the optimal closed-form solution to Eq. 23.

Proposition B.4 (Optimal ∞\infty-Rényi clipping.).

The solution to the optimization in Eq. 23 is given by the clipped truncation

pt∗​(y|y<t,x)=min⁡(c⋅pr​(y|y<t,x),ekt​ps​(y|y<t,x))∀y∈𝒱,\displaystyle p_{t}^{*}(y|y_{<t},x)=\min\left(c\cdot p_{r}(y|y_{<t},x),e^{k_{t}}p_{s}(y|y_{<t},x)\right)\quad\forall y\in\mathcal{V}, (28)

where cc is the unique scalar such that ∑y∈𝒱pt∗​(y)=1\sum_{y\in\mathcal{V}}p^{*}_{t}(y)=1.

Proof.

Observe that the safety constraint in Eq. 23 is equivalent to a pointwise probability ratio bound: p⁡(y|y<t,x)≤ekt​ps​(y|y<t,x)p(y|y_{<t},x)\leq e^{k_{t}}p_{s}(y|y_{<t},x) for all y∈𝒱y\in\mathcal{V}. Thus, we seek a single scalar cc such that the resulting normalized distribution satisfies the ratio ceiling for each token yy. Eq. 28 ensures that p∗​(y|y<t,x)≤ekt​ps​(y|y<t,x)p^{*}(y|y_{<t},x)\leq e^{k_{t}}p_{s}(y|y_{<t},x) by construction: for any token yy, either pt∗​(y|y<t,x)=ekt​ps​(y|y<t,x)p_{t}^{*}(y|y_{<t},x)=e^{k_{t}}p_{s}(y|y_{<t},x) (the constraint is active), or pt∗​(y|y<t,x)<ekt​ps​(y|y<t,x)p_{t}^{*}(y|y_{<t},x)<e^{k_{t}}p_{s}(y|y_{<t},x) (the constraint is inactive). Since the function f⁡(c)=∑ymin⁡(c⋅pr​(y|y<t,x),ekt​ps​(y|y<t,x))f(c)=\sum_{y}\min(c\cdot p_{r}(y|y_{<t},x),e^{k_{t}}p_{s}(y|y_{<t},x)) is continuous and non-decreasing in cc, with limc→0f⁡(c)=0\lim_{c\rightarrow 0}f(c)=0 and limc→∞∑yekt​ps​(y|y<t,x)=ekt≥1\lim_{c\rightarrow\infty}\sum_{y}e^{k_{t}}p_{s}(y|y_{<t},x)=e^{k_{t}}\geq 1, there exists some finite cc such that f⁡(c)=1f(c)=1 by the intermediate value theorem.

Moreover, this choice is optimal as any feasible pp with D∞(p∥pr)=logcD_{\infty}(p\,\|\,p_{r})=\log c must satisfy p⁡(y)≤min⁡(c​pr​(y|y<t,x),ekt​ps​(y|y<t,x))p(y)\leq\min(cp_{r}(y|y_{<t},x),e^{k_{t}}p_{s}(y|y_{<t},x)) for all yy, hence 1=∑y∈𝒱p⁡(y)≤f⁡(c)1=\sum_{y\in\mathcal{V}}p(y)\leq f(c). Therefore, the smallest cc with f⁡(c)≥1f(c)\geq 1 minimizes the objective, and our construction attains it by enforcing f⁡(c)=1f(c)=1.

In practice, this optimal cc can be efficiently found via 1D bisection search. ∎

Adaptive budget allocation design.

We can derive an analogous version of the adaptive per-token budget introduced in Eq. 7 that uses the ∞\infty-Rényi divergence function. At each decoding step t<Tmaxt<T_{\max}, the adaptive budget ktk_{t} is defined based on the remaining safety allowance (if it is negative, it is clamped to 0).

Proposition B.5 (Global safety of adaptive banking with 𝒟=D∞\mathcal{D}=D_{\infty}).

Let

at(y<t)≔D∞(pt∗(⋅∣y<t,x)∥ps,t(⋅∣y<t,x))=logmaxy∈𝒱pt∗​(y∣y<t,x)ps,t​(y∣y<t,x).\displaystyle a_{t}(y_{<t})\coloneqq D_{\infty}\!\Bigl(p_{t}^{*}(\cdot\mid y_{<t},x)\,\Big\|\,p_{s,t}(\cdot\mid y_{<t},x)\Bigr)=\log\max_{y\in\mathcal{V}}\frac{p_{t}^{*}(y\mid y_{<t},x)}{p_{s,t}(y\mid y_{<t},x)}. (29)

Further, let KK be the global safety budget up to TmaxT_{\max}, and set kk by Corollary 3.2. If, for each t<Tmaxt<T_{\max} and each history y<ty_{<t}, the adaptively allocated budget is

kt​(y<t)=max⁡(0,(t+1)​k−∑j=0t−1aj​(y<j)−δinit​(x)),\displaystyle k_{t}(y_{<t})=\max\Bigl(0,\;(t+1)k-\sum_{j=0}^{t-1}a_{j}(y_{<j})-\delta_{\mathrm{init}}(x)\Bigr), (30)

and that each step distribution pt∗(⋅∣y<t,x)p_{t}^{*}(\cdot\mid y_{<t},x) satisfies at​(y<t)≤kt​(y<t)a_{t}(y_{<t})\leq k_{t}(y_{<t}), then for any T≤TmaxT\leq T_{\max}, the induced sequence distribution p∗(y0:T−1∣x)=∏t=0T−1pt∗(yt∣y<t,x)p^{*}(y_{0:T-1}\mid x)=\prod_{t=0}^{T-1}p_{t}^{*}(y_{t}\mid y_{<t},x) satisfies the global guarantee D∞(p∗(⋅∣x)∥ps(⋅∣x))≤KD_{\infty}(p^{*}(\cdot\mid x)\,\|\,p_{s}(\cdot\mid x))\leq K.

Proof.

Fix any sequence y0:T−1y_{0:T-1}, where T≤TmaxT\leq T_{\max}. Then, by the autoregressive product form,

logp∗(y0:T−1∣x)ps(y0:T−1∣x)\displaystyle\log\frac{p^{*}(y_{0:T-1}\mid x)}{p_{s}(y_{0:T-1}\mid x)} =∑t=0T−1log⁡pt∗​(yt∣y<t,x)ps,t​(yt∣y<t,x)≤∑t=0T−1at​(y<t),\displaystyle=\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}\log\frac{p_{t}^{*}(y_{t}\mid y_{<t},x)}{p_{s,t}(y_{t}\mid y_{<t},x)}\;\leq\;\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}a_{t}(y_{<t}), (31)

since each summand is bounded by the per-step maximum defining at​(y<t)a_{t}(y_{<t}). Next, define the partial sums St≔∑j=0taj​(y<j)S_{t}\coloneqq\sum_{j=0}^{t}a_{j}(y_{<j}). We will show by induction that

St≤max⁡(0,(t+1)​k−δinit​(x))∀t∈{0,…,T−1}.\displaystyle S_{t}\leq\max\bigl(0,\;(t+1)k-\delta_{\mathrm{init}}(x)\bigr)\qquad\forall t\in\{0,\dots,T-1\}. (32)
Base case (t=0t=0).

By assumption S0=a0​(y<0)≤k0​(y<0)=max⁡(0,k−δinit​(x))S_{0}=a_{0}(y_{<0})\leq k_{0}(y_{<0})=\max(0,k-\delta_{\mathrm{init}}(x)), which is (32) for t=0t=0.

Inductive step (t≥1t\geq 1).

Assume (32) holds for t−1t-1. Using at​(y<t)≤kt​(y<t)a_{t}(y_{<t})\leq k_{t}(y_{<t}) and the definition of ktk_{t},

St\displaystyle S_{t} =St−1+at​(y<t)≤St−1+max⁡(0,(t+1)​k−St−1−δinit​(x))\displaystyle=S_{t-1}+a_{t}(y_{<t})\leq S_{t-1}+\max\bigl(0,\;(t+1)k-S_{t-1}-\delta_{\mathrm{init}}(x)\bigr) (33)
=max⁡(St−1,(t+1)​k−δinit​(x)).\displaystyle=\max\bigl(S_{t-1},\;(t+1)k-\delta_{\mathrm{init}}(x)\bigr). (34)

Let A≔(t+1)​k−δinit​(x)A\coloneqq(t+1)k-\delta_{\mathrm{init}}(x). If A<0A<0, then t​k−δinit​(x)<0tk-\delta_{\mathrm{init}}(x)<0 so by the inductive hypothesis St−1≤max⁡(0,t​k−δinit​(x))=0S_{t-1}\leq\max(0,tk-\delta_{\mathrm{init}}(x))=0, hence St−1=0S_{t-1}=0 and St≤0=max⁡(0,A)S_{t}\leq 0=\max(0,A). If A≥0A\geq 0, then St≤St−1+max⁡(0,A−St−1)≤A=max⁡(0,A)S_{t}\leq S_{t-1}+\max(0,A-S_{t-1})\leq A=\max(0,A). Therefore St≤max⁡(0,A)=max⁡(0,(t+1)​k−δinit​(x))S_{t}\leq\max(0,A)=\max\bigl(0,(t+1)k-\delta_{\mathrm{init}}(x)\bigr), completing the inductive step.

Thus (32) holds for all tt, and in particular

∑t=0T−1at​(y<t)=ST−1≤max⁡(0,T​k−δinit​(x))≤T​k≤Tmax​k=K.\displaystyle\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}a_{t}(y_{<t})=S_{T-1}\leq\max(0,Tk-\delta_{\mathrm{init}}(x))\leq Tk\leq T_{\max}k=K. (35)

Since this bound holds for every y0:T−1y_{0:T-1}, taking the maximum over sequences gives

D∞(p∗(⋅∣x)∥ps(⋅∣x))=logmaxy0:T−1p∗(y0:T−1∣x)ps(y0:T−1∣x)≤K.\displaystyle D_{\infty}\!\bigl(p^{*}(\cdot\mid x)\,\|\,p_{s}(\cdot\mid x)\bigr)=\log\max_{y_{0:T-1}}\frac{p^{*}(y_{0:T-1}\mid x)}{p_{s}(y_{0:T-1}\mid x)}\leq K. (36)
