B.4 Implementation Details

Prefix debt.

We compute δinit​(x)\delta_{\mathrm{init}}(x) excluding all special tokens (e.g., <BOS>, <EOS>, <PAD>).

For token-level decoding, we implement a prefill trick for efficient computation: the forward passes used to compute δinit​(x)\delta_{\mathrm{init}}(x) are reused from the initial generation prefill, ensuring no additional latency behind the logit comparison itself. To reduce memory overhead, we employ a logit-gather trick: rather than storing the full vocabulary-sized tensors (𝐙∈ℝB×L×V\mathbf{Z}\in\mathbb{R}^{B\times L\times V}, with BB as batch size, LL as maximum sequence length, and VV as vocabulary size) for both models, we compute log-probabilities on the fly and immediately gather the values corresponding to the input tokens x0:L−1x_{0:L-1}. This reduces the peak memory complexity of the debt calculation from O⁡(L​V)O(LV) to O⁡(L)O(L) per sequence. Finally, we run inference on two GPUs by loading one model per GPU and performing the two forward passes in parallel, independently on each device, which is beneficial to the wall-clock efficiency.

For byte-level decoding, we find it empirically helpful to scale prefix debt to token-equivalent units by multiplying by a factor of 4 (as our byte-to-token conversion factor is 4). This enables direct comparison to token-level prefix debt. We also employ KV-cache reuse and a logit-gather optimization that stores only the log-probability of the actual byte at each position, reducing memory from 𝒪⁡(L​V)\mathcal{O}(LV) to 𝒪⁡(L)\mathcal{O}(L).

Optimization.

To solve for the optimal mixing weight γ∈[0,1]\gamma\in[0,1] at each decoding step, we implement a vectorized safeguarded Newton-Raphson solver with bracketing and bisection (a maximum of 20 Newton iterations plus a short feasibility-projection bisection), ensuring that the returned γ\gamma is numerically feasible. While the models themselves reside in bfloat16 for memory efficiency, the entire optimization loop is performed in float32. We apply the Newton solver only after the raw logits from prp_{r} and psp_{s} have been passed through logit processors and warpers (e.g., repetition penalty and temperature); this way, we ensure that the resulting fused distribution (which we sample from) strictly respects the per-step safety constraint.

Appendix C Experiment Details

C.1 Pretraining TinyComma 1.8B

One of our contributions is TinyComma 1.8B, a decoder-only LM trained on entirely permissively licensed data from the Common Pile (Kandpal et al., 2025). Unlike the Comma 7B models introduced by Kandpal et al. (2025), TinyComma 1.8B shares the same 128K-vocabulary tokenizer as the Llama 3 model family (Grattafiori et al., 2024).

We use the lingua (Videau et al., 2024) pre-training framework and train beyond Chinchilla-optimality (Hoffmann et al., 2022) for 169.5B tokens on the Common Pile. Pretraining consists of two stages: (1) a 156B-token general training stage over the entire Common Pile, following domain weights specified by Kandpal et al. (2025), and (2) a 13.5B-token cooldown stage on a weighted mixture of three high-quality domains (70% Wikimedia, 15% DOAB, and 15% of Data Provenance Initiative data) from the Common Pile. Table 3 shows model configuration details, and Table 4 shows training hyperparameters for both stages. Our hardware is a single node of 8 140-GiB H200 GPUs.

We benchmark TinyComma 1.8B and other models on standard language evaluation tasks in Fig. 7. Among these tasks, TinyComma 1.8B is the most performant open model for its size, which we attribute to the high quality of the Common Pile. We did not conduct an expansive hyperparameter or data mixture sweep, as the intent of this work is not to produce the best small open LM. Nevertheless, Fig. 7 shows that TinyComma 1.8B outperforms other psp_{s} of its size range, and only underperforms against the larger and more extensively-trained Comma 7B models. We publicly release our TinyComma 1.8B to support further research in this direction.

C.2 ByteSampler Integration

Our AnchoredByte Decoding leverages the recently proposed ByteSampler (Hayase et al., 2025) framework, which was originally proposed to solve the Prompt Boundary Problem (PBP). ByteSampler is an inference-time procedure that facilitates the efficient and lossless conversion of any LM (with a BPE tokenizer) into a byte-level model.

Unlike token-level vocabularies, the 256-dimensional byte space is highly sparse. At an arbitrary decoding step ii, some bytes may represent invalid UTF-8 continuations or are unreachable from the current tokenizer state, resulting in p~s​(b)=0\tilde{p}_{s}(b)=0 or p~r​(b)=0\tilde{p}_{r}(b)=0. To prevent numerical instability, we restrict the optimization to the support of p~s\tilde{p}_{s}, and drop bytes where p~r=p~s=0\tilde{p}_{r}=\tilde{p}_{s}=0, which never affect the objective or constraint.

C.3 Prefix Debt in Anchored Decoding

Sweeping the memorization window nn.

In Fig. 8, we sweep various values for nn (the memorization window for prefix debt calculation), using (ps,pr)={TinyComma 1.8B, Llama 3.1 70B}(p_{s},p_{r})=\{\textrm{TinyComma 1.8B{}, Llama 3.1 70B}\}. While Anchored Decoding consistently benefits from prefix debt—every setting with n>0n>0 achieves a strictly better trade-off than the n=0n=0 baseline—the trade-off curves in our sweep are largely insensitive to the choice of nn. As smaller nn may overreact to a a few spurious outliers (i.e., tokenization artifacts, rare names) and trigger unnecessarily large cold-starts, while larger nn dilute the tail signal (as shown with our AvgDebt ablation in Sec. 5.2), we set n=5n=5 for the prefix debt as a simple default.

Higher prefix debt correlates with stronger copyright-copying indicators.

Fig. 9 shows several overlap-based indicators of potential copyright copying versus prefix-debt decile, using token-level model pair {TinyComma 1.8B, Llama 3.1 70B}\{\textrm{TinyComma 1.8B{}, Llama 3.1 70B}\}. We observe that for all choices of nn, the prefix debt largely correlates with the metric shift.

Appendix D Evaluation

D.1 Decoding Hyper-parameters

Unless otherwise stated, we use a default temperature of 0.7 for our main experiments. and a repetition penalty of 1.1 and 1.05 when generating from Books and Bios, respectively.

D.2 Baseline details

System.

Following Wei et al. (2024), we use Mosaic’s DBRX system prompt (The Mosaic Research Team, 2024) (shown in Table 5), which has been found to achieve the best copyright prevention among others, and has been adopted as a default baseline by other work (Zhang et al., 2025b). We prepend it to all prompts.

RCAD (Wei et al., 2024).

At generation step tt and with query xx, RCAD has the model θ\theta take two forward passes—one including the context cc, and one without—to compute a new next-token distribution that downweights the influence of copyrighted context: yt∼softmax[(1+α)logitθ(⋅|x,y<t)−αlogitθ(⋅|c,y<t)]y_{t}\sim\textrm{softmax}[(1+\alpha)\textrm{logit}_{\theta}(\cdot|x,y_{<t})-\alpha\textrm{logit}_{\theta}(\cdot|c,y_{<t})], where α∈[0,1]\alpha\in[0,1] is a hyper-parameter. We evaluate RCAD using prp_{r}.

MemFree (Ippolito et al., 2023).

While MemFree originally assumes a global blocklist over LM pre-training corpora (this can be efficiently done using Bloom Filters), we do not know the data provenance of the prp_{r} used in this experiment. Thus, we construct a quasi-global nn-gram blocklist (from the retrieved contexts of all samples) upfront before generation. We evaluate MemFree using prp_{r}.

Forming retrieved context.

Both MemFree and RCAD require a blocklist of copyrighted sequences that is supplied at inference time. Since blocklist construction is a design choice, we follow prior copyright evaluation work (Wei et al., 2024) and adopt an efficient retrieval-based procedure in order to reflect realistic deployment where auxiliary text sources (e.g., from retrieval) may contain protected content that should not be copied.

Namely, we construct task-specific blocklists by retrieving from quasi-oracle datastores: the Books3 portion of the Pile (Gao et al., 2020) for copyright evaluation, and a 2018 Wikipedia dump released by Karpukhin et al. (2020) for factuality evaluation. We use a retrieval toolkit implementation from Yen (2025), and take gte-Qwen2-1.5B-Instruct (Li et al., 2023b) as the embedding model, and FAISS (Johnson et al., 2019) to construct a flat dense index over the datastore.

Each input query is prepended with an instruction prompt (Instruct: Given a web search query, retrieve relevant passages that answer the query\nQuery:") before encoding. We embed with last-token pooling and L2 normalization. During evaluation, the top-1 retrieved document for each sample is taken as blocklisted context. The mean top-1 retrieval score (cosine similarity between L2-normalized embeddings) is 0.818 on Books3 and 0.649 on Wikipedia, suggesting that retrieved documents are sufficiently semantically related to the queries.

CP-Fuse (Abad et al., 2025).

CP-Fuse is a KK-NAF-inspired algorithm that similarly solves for a per-step model fusion distribution. CP-Fuse was originally designed for models p(1),p(2)p^{(1)},p^{(2)} of comparable utility trained on mutually exclusive dataset shards—an assumption seldom met by off-the-shelf LLMs. Intuitively, this disjoint-shard assumption supports a setting which potentially sensitive or protected content is distributed across references, without requiring the practitioner to explicitly label which training examples are problematic.

In our asymmetric safe–risky setting, we use a different instantiation: psp_{s} is trained only on permissively licensed text (so it is assumed to exclude all copyrighted sources), while prp_{r} may contain such sources. We therefore apply CP-Fuse as an inference-time fusion baseline on (ps,pr)(p_{s},p_{r}), noting that this use departs from CP-Fuse’s original theoretical assumptions.

Unlike Anchored Decoding, which follows a user-defined safety budget KK, CP-Fuse dynamically minimizes the per-token divergence budget kk at every decoding step.

Formally, at timestep tt, with input prompt xx and prefix history y<ty_{<t}, it solves for the following distribution (denote pt∗:=pt∗(⋅|y<t,x)p^{*}_{t}:=p_{t}^{*}(\cdot|y_{<t},x), and analogously for pt(i)p^{(i)}_{t}):

pt∗\displaystyle p^{*}_{t} =arg​minqt,k≥0ks.t.∀i:\displaystyle=\argmin_{q_{t},k\geq 0}k\quad\textrm{s.t.}\quad\forall i: (37)
DK​L(qt∥\displaystyle D_{KL}(q_{t}\,\|\, OPENpt(i))+log⁡(p∗​(y<t|x)p(i)​(y<t|x))≤k,\displaystyle p^{(i)}_{t})+\log\left(\tfrac{p^{*}(y_{<t}|x)}{p^{(i)}(y_{<t}|x)}\right)\leq k,

where pt(i):=p(i)(⋅∣y<t,x)p^{(i)}_{t}:=p^{(i)}(\cdot\mid y_{<t},x), and p∗​(y<t∣x)p^{*}(y_{<t}\mid x) denotes the prefix probability under the fused autoregressive distribution induced by the previously chosen conditionals {pj∗}j<t\{p_{j}^{*}\}_{j<t} (and analogously for p(i)​(y<t∣x)p^{(i)}(y_{<t}\mid x)). Intuitively, this approach seeks an optimal distribution p∗p^{*} that minimizes the maximum total divergence accumulated from each reference model p(i)p^{(i)} over the entire sequence.

We use the official implementation released by Abad et al. (2025) and follow their default hyper-parameter settings (e.g., a grid size of 10).

TokenSwap (Prashant et al., 2025).

We use the same seed list of words as the original work in Table 6. Note that each word is preceded by a whitespace, as functional words commonly have space-prefixed representations in modern subword vocabularies.

Adapting baselines to the byte level.

We instantiate all baselines except TokenSwap to the byte level via ByteSampler when evaluating in a mismatched-tokenizer (ps,pr)(p_{s},p_{r}) evaluation setting.

For System, we prepend the system prompt to the input and decode at the byte level. In MemFree, we detect nn-gram overlap in the byte space; to maintain a comparable granularity, we scale the reported token-level nn by a factor of 4. For RCAD and CP-Fuse, we apply the original methods to the induced next-byte distributions and find them effective.

Finally, TokenSwap is inherently token-level and does not directly extend to byte-level decoding. It relies on a set of common seed tokens manually curated by Prashant et al. (2025), most of which can be tokenized consistently across our choice of tokenizers. We therefore evaluate TokenSwap in token space.

In our experiments, ps=p_{s}{=}TinyComma 1.8B uses the Llama 3 tokenizer and shares identical tokenizations for all seed tokens with our choices of prp_{r}: Llama 3.1 70B, Qwen 2.5 72B, and Llama 4 Scout 17B×\times16E. However, with ps=p_{s}{=}Comma 7B, we find that the following seed tokens are not mapped identically: ’ to’, ’ and’, ’ of’, ’ in’, ’ an’, ’ me’. We exclude these tokens for that setting.

D.3 Copyright infringement

Metrics.

We consider these six metrics for assessing copyright infringement, and follow the implementations from Chen et al. (2024); Wei et al. (2024):

  • •

    ROUGE-1 ≥τ\geq\tau: ROUGE-1 is the overlap of unigrams between hypothesis and reference texts (after Porter stemming). We report the fraction of examples whose ROUGE-1 F1F_{1} exceeds τ=0.4\tau=0.4.

  • •

    ROUGE-L ≥τ\geq\tau: ROUGE-L is the non-contiguous longest common subsequence at the token level (after Porter stemming) between hypothesis and reference texts. We report the fraction of examples whose ROUGE-L F1F_{1} exceeds τ=0.4\tau=0.4.

  • •

    Word-level Longest Common Substring (Word-level LCS): The longest matching contiguous word span between reference and generation.

  • •

    Character-level Longest Common Substring (Char-level LCS): The longest contiguous character span shared by reference and generation.

  • •

    Word-level Accumulated Common Substrings (ACS): The total length of a greedy set of non-overlapping contiguous copied word spans with minimum length 6.

  • •

    MinHash: The MinHash-estimated Jaccard similarity of 3-word shingles.

For word-based metrics, we perform a normalization step that involves converting all text to lowercase, and truncate to the first 100 word tokens before scoring.

D.4 Utility

Fluency.

Following Chen et al. (2024), we evaluate generation fluency via LLM-as-a-judge (Zheng et al., 2023) using the Prometheus-Eval (Kim et al., 2024) framework. Prometheus allows for user-defined instruction rubrics, and uses LMs to score outputs from 1 to 5. We again adopt gpt-4.1-mini as our LLM backbone; while we have experimented using less-powerful open-source models, we find that they tend to conflate protected continuations with more fluent output. Our fluency rubric is defined in Table 7.

Long-form factuality.

We evaluate factuality in long-form generation using an implementation of FActScore (Min et al., 2023) that leverages recent improvements from Song et al. (2024).

FActScore consists of (1) claim extraction: using an LLM to decompose generations into atomic, verifiable claims, (2) evidence retrieval: fetching relevant evidence for each individual claim from a reliable knowledge bank, and (3) claim verification: using an LLM to score whether each individual claim is supported or unsupported by the retrieved context. The final metric is factual precision: the fraction of claims that are supported by the evidence.

For (1) and (3), we adopt OpenAI’s gpt-4.1-mini as our LLM backbone. Claim extraction is conducted in a sliding-window format to extricate self-contained, verifiable statements (Song et al., 2024). For (2), we retrieve the top-5 snippets from Google Search (via the Serper API1111 11 https://serper.dev) for each claim.

As is standard, we evaluate FActScore on a biography generation task for 183 historical individuals of varying degrees of notability. Given a particular entity, we use the prompt "Write a factual biography about {entity}. Include only factual information that you are confident in.\n Biography:".

D.5 Efficiency

Arithmetic FLOPS analysis.

First, we provide a theoretical estimate for Anchored Decoding decoding in terms of floating point operations (FLOPs) per generated token. Following Kaplan et al. (2020); Liu et al. (2022), we estimate that a decoder-only Transformer LM with NN parameters uses 2​N2N FLOPS per token for the inference forward pass, excluding smaller contributions from attention or softmax constants. For a risky model prp_{r} and safe model psp_{s}, define their parameter counts to be NrN_{r} and NsN_{s}, respectively. Assume a shared vocabulary size VV. Let the prompt length be LL, the number of generated tokens be TT, and the average number of solver iterations be II.

Anchored Decoding consists of three components: (1) per-step forward passes, (2) prefix debt computation, and (3) logit fusion with a KL-constrained solver.

(1) Forward passes. During decoding, Anchored Decoding runs one forward pass of prp_{r} and one of psp_{s} per generated token, for an estimated 2​(Nr+Ns)2(N_{r}+N_{s}) FLOPs/token.

(2) Prefix debt (with efficient prefill reuse). Prefix debt is computed once per request from the logits produced by the same two-model prefill that initializes KV caches for decoding with both prp_{r} and psp_{s}. Thus, prefix debt introduces no additional model forward passes beyond the two-model prefill already required by Anchored Decoding. Its incremental arithmetic cost is dominated by token-/vocab-level reductions (e.g., logsumexps and gathers) performed over the prompt, which we upper bound as 𝒪⁡(L​V)\mathcal{O}(LV) operations, or 𝒪⁡(L​V/T)\mathcal{O}(LV/T) when amortized over the TT generated tokens. This term becomes most relevant when TT is small (e.g., in very short generations), but not in typical usage with moderate-to-long continuations.

(3) Logit fusion. Logit fusion entails updating the budget, solving for optimal interpolation weights using a safeguarded Newton solver, and normalizing. This process is dominated by vocabulary-sized reductions; the per-step cost scales as 𝒪⁡(I​V)\mathcal{O}(IV) operations per generated token. This term is negligible in arithmetic FLOPs relative to the model forward passes.

Putting these together, the amortized FLOPs per generated token Anchored Decoding is estimated as

FLOPs/token≈ 2​(Nr+Ns)+2​(Nr+Ns)​LT⏟amortized two-model prefill+𝒪⁡(L​VT)+𝒪⁡(I​V),\mathrm{FLOPs/token}\;\approx\;2(N_{r}+N_{s})\;+\;\underbrace{2(N_{r}+N_{s})\frac{L}{T}}_{\text{amortized two-model prefill}}\;+\;\mathcal{O}\!\left(\frac{LV}{T}\right)\;+\;\mathcal{O}(IV), (38)

and in practice, for billion-parameter LMs, the forward-pass term 2​(Nr+Ns)2(N_{r}+N_{s}) dominates the arithmetic FLOP count.

Token-level wall-clock measurements.

In additional to a theoretical FLOPs analyses, we additionally measure the wall-clock efficiency of each decoding method under a standardized, token-level inference regime. All experiments are conducted on 2 141GiB H200 GPUs without CPU offloading.

We generate up to Tmax=200T_{\max}{=}200 new tokens at temperature 0.7 with a batch size of 4, and report averages over 3 runs after two warm-up iterations. For each run, we generate using the first 50 prompts from both the Books and Bios domains.

To decouple prompt-processing overhead from autoregressive decoding costs, we measure Time-to-First-Token (TTFT) and decode throughput. TTFT is computed on a single prompt (batch size 1) by timing a 1-token generation call (prefill plus one decode step). To isolate pure decode throughput, we time generation under a 1-token configuration (t1t_{1}) and a TT-token configuration (tTt_{T}). The decode-only throughput is then estimated by canceling the common prefill cost:

DecodeTok/s=NT−N1tT−t1,\displaystyle\mathrm{DecodeTok/s}=\frac{N_{T}-N_{1}}{t_{T}-t_{1}}, (39)

where NTN_{T} and N1N_{1} denote the total tokens generated in each configuration, respectively. Finally, we report TTFT, throughput overhead (TPSpr/TPS\mathrm{TPS}_{p_{r}}/\mathrm{TPS}) relative to prp_{r}, and FLOPs estimate for each setting.

Byte-level wall-clock measurements.

We report wall-clock measurements of all baselines implemented in ByteSampler in Table 8. We follow roughly the same settings as Sec. D.5, except we generate up to a maximum byte size of 200 for 3 runs. We additionally report AnchoredByte Decoding results without prefix debt δinit​(x)\delta_{\mathrm{init}}(x).

AnchoredByte Decoding incurs higher TTFB and a worse TPS ratio than its token-level counterpart as our byte-level code is not as well-optimized as the token-level case. First, the full 70B model and its tree-inference state on a single 140 GiB GPU without out-of-memory errors. Consequently, we must shard the 70B model across GPUs, which introduces inter-GPU communication overhead and slows throughput.

Second, computing the prefix debt makes the TTFB considerably slower (3566.8 vs. 186.3 ms). Prefix debt requires computing the log probabilities at every byte position in the prompt under both models, resulting in 𝒪⁡(L)\mathcal{O}(L) computation (for a prompt of length LL) with a much larger constant factor, before the first byte can even be generated. Unlike token-level prefix debt, which can reuse the standard prefill, byte-level computation requires additional BPE tree decomposition at each position to convert token probabilities to byte probabilities. Even with caching, this per-position tree computation is significantly more expensive than a standard prefill pass.

We note several workarounds: if the prompts are known in advance, we may precompute the prefix LLRs and load them on the fly for prefix debt computation. Another option is to omit the prefix debt entirely, as according to Fig. 3, δinit​(x)\delta_{\mathrm{init}}(x) leads to a small but consistent trade-off improvement.

Appendix E Additional Results

E.1 Adaptive Budgeting Handles Non-uniform Risk

Fig. 10 shows representative Copyright generation trajectories under Anchored Decoding (token-level) and AnchoredByte Decoding (byte-level) for various kk (with Tmax=200,Bmax=800T_{\max}=200,B_{\max}=800). We plot the realized spend KL(pt∗∥ps)\mathrm{KL}(p_{t}^{*}\|p_{s}) (blue), the diagnostic KL(pr∥ps)\mathrm{KL}(p_{r}\|p_{s}) (green, where shown), and the adaptive allowance ktk_{t} (magenta) relative to the nominal cap kk (red).

At the token level, k=0.1k=0.1 yields a conservative cold start: ktk_{t} is floored at 00 for much of the prefix-debt window, forcing pt∗p_{t}^{*} to track psp_{s} closely. At k=1.5k=1.5, budgeting becomes dynamic: ktk_{t} banks allowance during low-risk steps and releases it to accommodate occasional memorization spikes, allowing KL(pt∗∥ps)\mathrm{KL}(p_{t}^{*}\|p_{s}) to exceed the nominal cap while remaining globally feasible. At k=3.0k=3.0, the constraint is rarely binding and pt∗≈prp_{t}^{*}\approx p_{r}, reflected by KL(pt∗∥ps)≈KL(pr∥ps)\mathrm{KL}(p_{t}^{*}\|p_{s})\approx\mathrm{KL}(p_{r}\|p_{s}).

The byte-level view exhibits the same pattern at finer temporal resolution: risk manifests as sharper, more localized spikes, and ktk_{t} rises rapidly during low-risk stretches. Since many byte steps incur near-zero divergence, the model typically accrues budget faster at the same kk than in the token-level regime.

E.2 Long-tail Knowledge vs. kk

We show that Anchored Decoding may unintentionally suppress legitimate long-tail factual recall. Rare entities are less likely to be memorized by psp_{s} (which, in our work, is orders of magnitude smaller than prp_{r}, and typically not as well-trained). Thus, enforcing proximity to psp_{s} may also disproportionately suppress correct but uncommon facts. To probe this effect, we return to biography generation on Bios and stratify prompts by entity frequency (from Very Rare to Very Frequent) using labels provided by Min et al. (2023). For each bucket, we report average FActScore claim precision as a function of the budget kk (log scale), with psp_{s} and prp_{r} as reference points. We decode at the token level with {TinyComma 1.8B, Llama 3.1 70B} and Tmax=200T_{\max}=200. Fig. 11 shows a consistent trend: increasing kk improves factual precision across all buckets as Anchored Decoding shifts mass from psp_{s} toward prp_{r}, but the gains are strongly frequency-dependent and saturate at prp_{r}’s bucket-specific ceiling. Frequent entities recover quickly, while Rare and Very Rare entities improve more slowly and plateau at substantially lower precision as prp_{r} itself is unreliable on the long tail. Meanwhile, psp_{s} remains uniformly low across buckets, suggesting limited factual coverage regardless of frequency.

E.3 Non-literal Copying Results

While literal copying is the primary focus of our work, we also show that Anchored Decoding can alleviate non-literal copying, which, within a literary context, is the generation of the same incidental characters, events, or plot elements as an original work, despite differences in surface form (Chen et al., 2024).

In a small-scale experiment, we adopt the character copying evaluation of Chen et al. (2024). This benchmark extracts a set of key characters from each popular novel from its CliffsNotes summary. Models are prompted to generate an open-ended story, given a plot summary sentence, e.g., “Theo and his mother visit the Metropolitan Museum of Art.”.

We then measure whether these character names appear in the model’s generation via exact string match. Following their protocol, we report character overlap, or the fraction of samples for which the number of matched character names exceeds 3. We also report the non-verbatim fluency of the model generation, which is scored following Sec. D.4.

We use the token-level model pair {TinyComma 1.8B, Llama 3.1 70B}. We sweep Anchored Decoding across various kk, and disable the prefix debt, since it is primarily designed to curb literal copying and we find it can hurt fluency in this non-literal setting. We additionally report our context-less baselines (System, TokenSwap, CP-Fuse).

Fig. 12 shows results. Anchored Decoding defines the Pareto frontier (in the upper-right region), attaining the best tradeoff between fluency and non-literal copying mitigation.

Beyond literary settings, non-literal copying is also relevant for tasks such as translation (e.g., “Give me the first chapter of Harry Potter in Spanish”) or rule-based transformations (e.g., “Give me the first chapter of The Goldfinch, but in all-caps”). However, evaluating non-literal copying in the form of character or event overlap is typically a non-issue in domains such as news articles, where the underlying events, subjects, and timelines are factual and therefore generally not protected by copyright. This indicates that addressing non-verbatim copying may warrant a more task-aware approach that is tailored to the domain and transformation. We defer a more careful and exhaustive evaluation of non-literal copying to future work.
